title: Python Sets
relevance: Sets are a common interview and OA topic for uniqueness, fast membership checks, and mathematical set operations on collections.

phases.goal: Establish what a set is, its mutability rules, and how it is created correctly.

must_hit.point: A set is an unordered collection of unique elements; the set itself is mutable but its elements must be immutable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says unordered/no duplicates, you can add/remove from the set, but elements must be hashable immutables like ints, floats, strings, or tuples.

must_hit.point: An empty set must be created with set(); using {} creates an empty dictionary, not a set.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate warns that s = {} is a dict and shows s = set() for an empty set.

must_hit.point: Sets cannot contain mutable types such as lists, dicts, or other sets; doing so raises a TypeError for an unhashable type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects nested lists/sets inside a set and mentions unhashable/TypeError.

must_hit.point: Python treats True as 1 and False as 0, so True is a duplicate of 1 inside a set and is ignored.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains {1, True, ...} keeps 1 and drops True as a duplicate.

probes: What is a Python set, and what rules apply to the set versus its elements?
How do you create an empty set, and what goes wrong with curly braces alone?

hints.1: Think about order, uniqueness, and what can change after creation.
hints.2: Separate the mutability of the container from the hashability of its members; also contrast set() with {}.
hints.3: Say: unordered unique items; set mutable, elements immutable; empty set via set() because {} is a dict; no lists/dicts/sets as elements; True equals 1 for membership uniqueness.

phases.goal: Cover how elements are accessed, added, removed, and combined via set operations and methods.

must_hit.point: Sets do not support indexing or slicing; access is by iteration or membership tests with in / not in.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says subscripting raises TypeError and describes looping or in checks instead.

must_hit.point: add() inserts one element; update() adds multiple elements from an iterable such as a list, tuple, or another set.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts single-element add with update taking an iterable.

must_hit.point: discard() removes an item without error if missing; remove() raises KeyError if missing; pop() removes and returns an arbitrary item; clear() empties the set; del deletes the set object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes discard vs remove (KeyError), pop as arbitrary, clear vs del.

must_hit.point: Union (|), intersection (&), difference (-), and symmetric difference (^) implement the standard mathematical set operations; method forms exist that either return a new set or update in place (e.g. union vs update, intersection vs intersection_update).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps operators to meanings and notes returning-new vs in-place *_update / update variants.

must_hit.point: Relation helpers include isdisjoint (null intersection), issuperset, and issubset; sorted(s) returns a sorted list of the set's items.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names isdisjoint/issuperset/issubset and that sorted yields a list, not a set.

probes: How do you add and remove elements from a set, and how do the removal methods differ?
Walk through union, intersection, difference, and symmetric difference on two sets.

hints.1: Start with what you cannot do for access, then name the add/remove APIs.
hints.2: Contrast discard vs remove vs pop; then map | & - ^ to meanings and new-set vs in-place methods.
hints.3: No indexing; add/update; discard silent, remove KeyError, pop arbitrary, clear/del; | all, & common, - one-sided, ^ exclusive-or; mention relation checks and sorted returning a list.

phases.goal: Compare mutating vs non-mutating APIs and set vs frozenset when immutability or nesting is required.

must_hit.point: Prefer discard when absence should be silent; prefer remove when missing items should surface as KeyError.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks discard for soft delete and remove when the item is required to exist.

must_hit.point: Operator/method forms like union/intersection/difference/symmetric_difference return a new set, while update and the *_update methods mutate the receiver in place.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says non-update forms leave originals unchanged; update/intersection_update/etc. change s1.

must_hit.point: Use a frozenset when you need an immutable set usable as a dict key or as an element of another set; ordinary sets cannot nest inside sets.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains frozenset is immutable/hashable so set-of-frozensets works where set-of-sets fails.

probes: When would you choose discard over remove, or a returning set method over an in-place update?
Why would you use a frozenset instead of a set?

hints.1: Think about error signaling and whether callers need a new collection or a mutated one.
hints.2: Compare silent vs KeyError removal, then new-set APIs vs update/*_update, then hashability for nesting/keys.
hints.3: discard if missing OK, remove if missing is a bug; union etc. new set vs update mutating; frozenset for dict keys or elements inside another set.

phases.goal: Apply sets for membership, nesting via frozenset, and set comprehensions.

must_hit.point: Membership tests with in / not in on sets are much faster than the same checks on lists, which is a common reason to use a set.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites faster membership on sets versus lists for lookups.

must_hit.point: A set of sets is illegal, but a set of frozensets is valid because frozensets are immutable and hashable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows nested frozensets as the way to get a 2D-set-like structure.

must_hit.point: Set comprehensions build sets concisely with filters or transforms, similar to list comprehensions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes a comprehension with a condition or mapping (e.g. filtered values or squares) producing a set.

probes: When would you convert a list to a set in an interview problem?
How can you represent a set of sets in Python?
Show a set comprehension with a filter or transformation.

hints.1: Think about lookup speed and uniqueness, then about nesting constraints.
hints.2: Membership/dedup → set; nesting → frozenset elements; concise build → {expr for ... if ...}.
hints.3: Use sets for fast in checks and uniqueness; nest via frozenset; e.g. {i for i in range(...) if ...} or squares via comprehension.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: discard removes without error if the item is absent; remove raises KeyError if absent—choose based on whether missing membership is expected or a bug.

tradeoffs.topic: returning set methods vs in-place update/*_update
tradeoffs.strong_answer: union/intersection/difference/symmetric_difference (and operator forms) return a new set; update and intersection_update/difference_update/symmetric_difference_update mutate the original set in place.
set is mutable and supports add/remove/update/clear/pop/discard; frozenset is immutable, supports only read operations, and can be a dict key or an element of another set.
Testing membership with in/not in is much faster on sets than on lists, so convert to a set when repeated membership checks matter.

gotchas.trap: Writing s = {} expecting an empty set
gotchas.correction: {} creates an empty dictionary; use s = set() for an empty set.

gotchas.trap: Assuming True and 1 are distinct set elements
gotchas.correction: Python treats True as 1 (and False as 0), so True is ignored as a duplicate of 1.
Sets are unordered and not subscriptable; use iteration or in/not in.

gotchas.trap: Putting a list, dict, or set inside a set
gotchas.correction: Elements must be immutable/hashable; mutable containers raise TypeError: unhashable type.

gotchas.trap: Trying to build a set of sets for a 2D set
gotchas.correction: Inner sets are unhashable; use frozensets as elements instead.

gotchas.trap: Calling remove on a missing element
gotchas.correction: remove raises KeyError; use discard if absence should be silent.

gotchas.trap: Assuming pop() removes a predictable element
gotchas.correction: pop removes and returns an arbitrary item from the set.
